newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Masood forces begin major attack on key Afghan pass.
newsitem.headline: Masood forces begin major attack on key Afghan pass.

text.p: Forces of the ousted Afghan government launched a major attack early on Wednesday to capture the De Sabz pass, a strategic position just 10 km (6 miles) north of the Afghan capital Kabul.

Shells and rockets fired by Jamiat-i-Islami troops under the leadership of deposed government commander Ahmad Shah Masood pounded positions of the radical Islamic Taleban militia in hills above the pass nearly every minute.
Masood is trying to dislodge Taleban forces from Kabul nearly a month after the fundamentalist Islamic group captured the capital, giving it control of two-thirds of the country.
Control of the pass, which links the road from Masood-controlled territory to northeastern Kabul, would give Masood's forces command of heights vital for an advance on the capital.

"We are progressing," Mehrabodin Masstan, a spokesman for Masood, told reporters. "We have taken control of the high positions (on De Sabz pass) and we will soon clear the Taleban's remaining two positions."
"If we take control of this pass (De Sabz), we get very close to Kabul -- we will be only 10 km away," Masstan said.

Jamiat-i-Islami commanders in the village of Kalakan, around 25 km (18 miles) north of Kabul, said Masood's forces launched an artillery barrage at 4:00 a.m. (0030 GMT) and sent in troops to encircle Taleban troops on the pass.
"We're moving round to encircle them and we will move on Kabul, God willing," said Abdul Rahim Yusufi, a field commander clutching a walkie-talkie, in command of 300 men in Kalakan.
His men looked tired compared to a festive atmosphere on Tuesday in anticipation of the offensive.
They gazed blankly at puffs of dust kicked up by Jamiat-i-Islami shelling and ignored the Taleban's return fire which shook the ground in a nearby village.

Masstan said forces belonging to northern Uzbek chieftain Abdul Rashid Dostum had taken part in the attack and added that fighters deployed near a second important pass, Khair Khana, had mostly held fire on Wednesday.
The Khair Khana pass also leads to Kabul.
Orange flame spurted out of the back of a truck-mounted rocket launcher as Jamiat-i-Islami forces sent a rocket onto the barren hills below the snow-capped peaks of the Hindu Kush.
The rocket stirred up a column of sand and dust which floated over two old men in long robes and turbans placing grapes out to dry in the autumn sun.
"We're not firing that many rockets now," said the battery commander. "The Taleban are deserting the mountain."
